title: GARS Converter: Global Area Reference System
description: Convert between coordinates and GARS references with the GARS Converter — the coarse global grid used in aviation and planning contexts. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, GARS divides the world into 30-minute cells — each roughly 55 km tall — addressed by a compact designator, so a search area can be spoken over a radio without a single decimal.
quick_answer: The GARS Converter converts between map coordinates and Global Area Reference System references — the coarse global grid of 30-minute cells, subdivided into 15- and 5-minute areas, used in some aviation and planning contexts. Enter coordinates and read the cell designator — an area reference that survives radios and whiteboards.

faq: Is this an official DoD tool?
No — it is an independent converter implementing the published GARS structure for planning support and interoperability. Official operations use authorised NGA tools and current publications.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 coordinates, the reference frame GARS itself is defined over.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
GARS references name areas, not points — decimal thinking does not apply. Precision inside a cell belongs to coordinates or MGRS.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Cell corners convert to coordinates and paste as extents; designators travel as labels. GIS layers for GARS exist in defence GIS ecosystems.
GARS versus MGRS?
Area versus point: GARS tops out at 5′ areas (~9 km); MGRS refines to metres. Different jobs — search management versus position reporting.
Why the keypad layout?
The 3×3 subdivision mirrors a phone keypad so designators can be spoken and remembered — human factors engineered into a grid.
Polar handling?
Latitudinal bands cap at the poles in the standard's scheme; the converter follows the published banding rather than inventing polar cells.
Cell containing a coordinate — or all cells in an area?
Point-to-cell here; tiling an area with cells is a GIS operation the corners from this converter can seed.
Historical references?
GARS is a modern (2000s) standard — older documents use other area systems (GEOREF among them), each with its own converter logic.
Can a designator be wrong but plausible?
Yes — neighbouring cells differ by one character. Cross-check by converting back to coordinates and glancing at the map, the grid-user's standing habit.
Radio pronunciation?
Designators are read character by character in operations — another reason the system favours short, unambiguous strings.
